phaseR

longitudinal change as a switch between regimes

phaseR fits Bayesian models of change in longitudinal data, such as disease onset and recovery, treatment adoption or an ecological regime shift, in which each unit moves from a “before” regime to an “after” regime.

The package treats “before” and “after” as latent regimes and models two things jointly: the transition that moves a unit between regimes, and the outcome dynamics within each regime. The likelihood sums over the regime each observation may belong to, so the estimates do not condition on the realized transition. Splitting the data at the observed change point and comparing the two halves does condition on it, which biases the comparison whenever the chance of transitioning depends on the same covariates that drive the outcome. From a fit you can estimate regime effects and counterfactual outcomes, and decide which comparison answers your question. phaseR supports:

  • More than two regimes. Ordered phases such as phases("susceptible", "infected", "recovered"), with one transition() per consecutive pair.
  • Non-Gaussian outcomes. Gaussian, Poisson and binomial dynamics, set per phase.
  • Random effects. Random intercepts (1 | group), crossed (1 | site) + (1 | year), random slopes (1 + x | group) and nested (1 | site/plot).
  • Custom priors. prior() with normal(), student_t(), cauchy(), half_normal(), half_cauchy() and lkj().
  • Counterfactual effects. ate(), ite() and counterfactual() predict outcomes under covariate values that were never observed, integrating over phase uncertainty.
  • Model comparison. WAIC with waic() and compare_waic(), and leave-one-out cross-validation by Pareto-smoothed importance sampling with loo() and loo_compare().

The default backend is the No-U-Turn sampler (NUTS), an adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method, written in C++ with Rcpp, so no Stan, JAGS or other inference engine has to be installed. Why Conditioning on Realized Change Fails runs the before/after estimate and the phaseR estimate against a known truth on simulated data.

Installation

The package compiles C++ code. Install the build tools for your operating system first:

Operating system Build tools
Windows Rtools
macOS Run xcode-select --install in Terminal
Debian / Ubuntu Install r-base-dev

Check that R can find the compiler:

pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)

Then install phaseR:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/phaseR")

The C++ code is compiled with Rcpp to the C++17 standard and needs no system libraries.

Usage

  1. Declare the regimes with phases(), the transition model with transition() and the outcome model of each regime with dynamics(), and combine them with phase_model().
  2. Fit the model to long-format data (one row per unit and time) with fit_phaseR().
  3. Read the coefficients with summary(), and estimate effects with ate(), ite() or counterfactual().

sim_phaseR() simulates data with a unit identifier id, a time index time, a covariate x, an outcome y and the true phase. The transition depends on x, and each regime has its own regression of y on x:

library(phaseR)

dat <- sim_phaseR(n_units = 100, n_times = 5, seed = 42)

model <- phase_model(
  phases("inactive", "active"),
  transition("inactive", "active", ~ x),
  dynamics("inactive", y ~ x),
  dynamics("active", y ~ x)
)

fit <- fit_phaseR(model, data = dat, backend = "laplace", seed = 42)
summary(fit)
#> Phase Model Summary
#> Phases: inactive -> active
#> 
#> Transition coefficients:
#>                         mean   sd  2.5% median 97.5% Rhat    ESS
#> beta_trans_(Intercept) -0.92 0.24 -1.39  -0.92 -0.47   NA 996.64
#> beta_trans_x            0.42 0.25 -0.08   0.42  0.90   NA 862.56
#> 
#> Dynamics coefficients (inactive):
#>                           mean   sd  2.5% median 97.5% Rhat    ESS
#> beta_inactive_(Intercept) 9.88 0.08  9.72   9.88 10.03   NA 979.03
#> beta_inactive_x           0.06 0.07 -0.07   0.06  0.19   NA 993.48
#> 
#> Dynamics coefficients (active):
#>                          mean   sd  2.5% median 97.5% Rhat    ESS
#> beta_active_(Intercept)  7.95 0.15  7.65   7.96  8.24   NA 888.67
#> beta_active_x           -0.47 0.13 -0.72  -0.47 -0.22   NA 900.03
#> 
#> Variance parameters:
#>                    mean   sd  2.5% median 97.5% Rhat     ESS
#> log_sigma_inactive 0.04 0.05 -0.05   0.04  0.14   NA  944.09
#> log_sigma_active   0.41 0.06  0.30   0.40  0.52   NA 1082.53

backend = "laplace" approximates the posterior by a Gaussian at its mode and returns within a second. The default backend, "hmc", samples the posterior with the No-U-Turn sampler, and chains and iter set the number of chains and the iterations per chain:

fit <- fit_phaseR(model, data = dat, chains = 2, iter = 1000, seed = 42)

Why splitting at the change point is biased

Comparing the outcomes of units that transitioned, before against after, stratifies on a realized outcome. When units with certain covariate values are both more likely to transition and have different outcomes, the measured difference mixes the regime effect with that selection, and the bias does not shrink with more data.

phaseR writes down the full generative process instead: a logistic transition model for regime membership and an outcome model per regime, fitted jointly. The likelihood sums over the latent regime of every observation with a log-sum-exp over phase assignments, so the selection mechanism is part of the model. Why Conditioning on Realized Change Fails shows the bias on simulated data with a known effect.

Counterfactual effects

Because the transition and the dynamics are modelled together, a fit predicts outcomes under covariate values that were never observed, integrating over phase uncertainty. ate() returns the average effect of setting x to 1 against 0, with a 95% credible interval:

effect <- ate(fit, treatment_var = "x")
effect$ate
#> [1] -0.3821998
effect$ate_ci
#>        2.5%       97.5% 
#> -0.71036013 -0.06097235

counterfactual() predicts outcomes for new covariate values, and ite() returns the effect per unit:

counterfactual(fit, newdata = transform(dat, x = 1))
ite(fit, treatment_var = "x")

Models with more regimes

A model with three regimes declares the phases in order, one transition per consecutive pair and one outcome model per regime:

model <- phase_model(
  phases("susceptible", "infected", "recovered"),
  transition("susceptible", "infected", ~ exposure + age),
  transition("infected", "recovered", ~ treatment),
  dynamics("susceptible", y ~ 1),
  dynamics("infected", y ~ time_since_infection),
  dynamics("recovered", y ~ 1)
)

Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the GitHub issues. A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with reprex.
